svg.text: L
Lakko - cross-platform screen matrix
Every major screen on web, iOS and Android side by side, with the copy each client actually ships.
Drawn from the three clients' sources on 2026-09-21; sign-up and recovery rows redrawn 2026-10-02. Schematic, not pixel-accurate: read it for structure, copy and parity, not for spacing.
WEB - desktop, SolidJS
iOS - SwiftUI
ANDROID - Compose
PARITY NOTES
matches
wording / layout drift
real gap
1. First run / Welcome

g.text: An unauthenticated visit to / redirects straight
to Log in. The brand headline the phones show on
first run has nowhere to live.

svg.text: PARITY
iOS and Android are identical: logo,
'Lakko', 'Messages that stay between you.',
Create account / Log in.
Web has no Welcome screen at all - / goes to
Log in. The product's one-line promise is
never shown on web.
Fix is cheap: reuse AuthLayout's gradient
panel for a public landing at /.
2. Log in
PARITY
Same four controls everywhere: Username,
Password, Log in, Use passkey, plus 'Forgot
password?'.
The 'How Lakko protects your password'
explainer is on all three (web carries it on
both Log in and Create account).
Web shows 'Create account' in the footer,
iOS shows 'New to Lakko?', Android shows
nothing - three answers to one question.
3. Create account

g.text: device. You will get a recovery
Your password never leaves your device. You
will get a recovery phrase to write down next.
Already have an account? Log in
Your password never leaves your device. You
will get a recovery phrase to write down next.

Already have an account? Log in

Your password never leaves your device. You
will get a recovery phrase to write down next.

svg.text: PARITY
Field order, labels and hints are the same
on all three and come from one catalog:
Username, 'Name (optional)', Password,
Confirm password, Create account.
Web shows no username rule up front: it
echoes the handle live and speaks only when
the name is rejected. The phones show the
rule sentence under the field from the
start.
The sentence that announces the recovery
phrase sits under the title on web and iOS,
and below the button on Android.
'How Lakko protects your password' is on the
web form only; 'Already have an account? Log
in' is on web and iOS, Android has the back
arrow instead.
Nothing about recovery is chosen on this
form any more: the phrase, its check and the
passkey offer follow as steps 1 to 3.
4. Sign-up, step 1: the recovery phrase

g.text: back on a new device if you lose
Write them down in order and keep
These 12 words bring your account back on a new device
if you lose your password and your devices. Write them
down in order and keep them somewhere safe.
Do not keep them as a screenshot or in a plain text
file. Lakko cannot show them again.
These 12 words bring your account back on a new
device if you lose your password and your
devices. Write them down in order and keep them
Do not keep them as a screenshot or in a
plain text file. Lakko cannot show them
These 12 words bring your account back on a new
device if you lose your password and your
devices. Write them down in order and keep them
Anyone who has these words can read your
messages and act as you. Do not share them.
Do not keep them as a screenshot or in a plain
text file. Lakko cannot show them again.

svg.text: PARITY
12 numbered words on all three, numbered row
by row: 3 columns x 4 rows at phone width, 4
x 3 on a wide screen (the web card shown
here). Display, the check and typing the
phrase back all use this one order.
Same title, 'Step 1 of 3', lede and Copy on
all three. No shares, no 'More options': the
phrase is the only thing to save.
The button that leaves this step reads 'I
have written them down' on web and iOS and
'Continue' on Android.
Android shows two warning sentences ('Anyone
who has these words...' and the screenshot
one); web and iOS show the screenshot
sentence only.
Step 2 (not drawn) asks for three words at
random positions. Web adds an 'I understand
that losing these words...' checkbox before
Continue; the phones do not have it.
5. Sign-up, step 3: add a passkey

g.text: Add a passkey so you can sign in
Add a passkey so you can sign in with your face,
Let this passkey restore your keys?
Add a passkey so you can sign in with your
Let this passkey restore your keys?
Add a passkey so you can sign in with your
Let this passkey restore your keys?

svg.text: PARITY
Same step on all three: 'Add a passkey' or
'Not now'. It never blocks sign-up, and an
account without a username is not offered it
(the flow is then two steps).
Adding a passkey stores nothing by itself.
Where the platform can protect keys with it,
the opt-in question 'Let this passkey
restore your keys?' follows; otherwise a
line says the passkey signs in only.
Web offers the step only in a browser that
supports passkeys; the phones offer it to
every account with a username.
'Not now' is a text button on web and a
full-width secondary button on the phones.

svg.text: PARITY
Same two groups, same rows, same order and
same sentences on all three. 'Brings back
your chats': Another device (first),
Passkey, Recovery phrase. 'Signs you in on
this device': Three words from your phrase,
Authenticator code.
No row is hidden or badged from server
state. The one conditional row is local:
'Three words from your phrase' is listed
only on a device that holds the phrase and
the keys of its cached account, and the note
under the list names three words only when
the row is there.
The line under the title is 'Choose how.' on
web and iOS; Android names the cached
account ('Choose how to get back into
@anna.').
Footer: web has 'Remembered your password?
Log in'; iOS adds 'New to Lakko? Create
account'; Android has neither, only the back
arrow.
'Another device' is not the same act
everywhere: web asks for the username and a
six-digit code typed from the signed-in
device; iOS and Android show a QR code for
the other device to scan.
7. Recovery: three words

g.text: Type three words of your recovery
Type words 7, 3 and 12 of your recovery phrase.
This device checks the words itself and signs you in.
You then choose a new password.
Too many wrong tries. Try again in 14:59.

Type words 7, 3 and 12 of your recovery phrase.
This device checks the words itself and signs
you in. You then choose a new password.
Too many wrong tries. Try again in 14:59.
Type words 7, 3 and 12 of your recovery phrase.
This device checks the words itself and signs
you in. You then choose a new password.
Too many wrong tries. Try again in 14:59.

svg.text: PARITY
Same form on all three: no username field
(the cached account is named), three
numbered fields at positions drawn at random
and asked in the drawn order, 'Sign in'. The
device checks the words itself; nothing is
sent until they match.
Same budget on all three: a miss draws new
positions, clears the fields and shows the
tries left; the fifth miss starts a
15-minute pause with a countdown, and the
count survives a restart.
It signs in only, and says so on the form.
'Choose a new password' follows on all
three.
Web lays the three fields out in one row,
each with its number inside and the
placeholder 'word 7'; the phones stack three
labelled fields ('Word 7').
iOS repeats the row's subtitle under the
title; web and Android show the title alone.
8. Chats list

g.text: Select a chat to start messaging

svg.text: PARITY
The strongest parity in the product: same
title, same search, pinned / all grouping,
same swipe-or-menu actions (Pin, Mute,
Archive), same empty state 'No chats yet' +
'Start a chat'.
Same five destinations on all three: Chats,
Groups, Channels, Contacts, Settings.
Android places a floating action button for
New chat; iOS and web use a header +.
The design system's IA lists a top-level
'Calls' destination. No client has one - web
/calls redirects to Contacts and call links
live inside Contacts. Either the doc or the
three clients are wrong.
9. Conversation

g.text: Yes. I booked the table already.

svg.text: PARITY
Same header (avatar, name, @username, call /
video / more), same bubble shape, same
'Sent' / 'Read' state, same typing line,
same composer with attach + emoji + send.
Edit, Delete, React, reaction chips and the
'(edited)' / 'message deleted' markers exist
on all three; hover menu on web, long-press
on the phones - the documented divergence.
Group info opens a right-side members panel
on web, a sheet labelled 'Group info' on
iOS, and a screen labelled 'Details' on
Android. Three names for one surface.
10. New group

g.text: You will be the group's owner. You can add more people
Everyone in the group sees the name. Leave
it blank to title the group by its members.

svg.text: PARITY
Same shape: name field, contact picker with
checkmarks, one Create group button, same
refusal copy 'Accept this contact again to
add them to a group.'
Only iOS explains what an empty name does
('Leave it blank to title the group by its
members'). Web and Android leave the user
guessing.
The no-contacts empty state differs: web
'Add contacts first; a group starts from
people you already know', iOS points at 'the
Contacts tab', Android shows a 'Go to
Contacts' button.
11. Contacts

g.text: Hi, this is Alice from the conference.
Share a link with someone you want to
A call anyone with the link can ask to
Hi, this is Sergey from the meetup.

svg.text: PARITY
Same three jobs on all three: add by
username with an intro line, invite links,
call links. Requests carry Accept / Decline.
Web lays them out as three cards side by
side; the phones stack them under the
contact list, so 'Create call link' is below
the fold on a phone.
Invite links carry a label, an expiry preset
and a use limit on web and Android. iOS
offers only Create link / Copy / Share /
Revoke, so a link made on an iPhone silently
takes whatever the defaults are.
This screen is where Calls actually lives.
Nothing in the navigation says so.
12. Channels

g.text: Version 1.4 is out. Group names are end-to-end
We published the security notes for this release.
Calls now show the safety number on every platform.
Channels you create or subscribe to
Channels you create or subscribe to

svg.text: PARITY
Same model on all three: subscribed list,
find by @handle, create, join as
co-publisher, reader with posts, 'Waiting to
be let in...' while the publisher shares
access.
Search placeholder: '@my-channel' (web),
'Search or enter a @handle' (iOS), 'Find a
channel' (Android).
Name, handle and an optional description on
all three create flows; subscribers see the
name and the description.
13. In-call

g.text: Flip camera lives on the self tile, not in the bar
red = local flag only, no peer sees it
red = local flag only, no peer sees it

svg.text: PARITY
Same shell everywhere: title, timer, roster
tiles with a muted marker, participants
list, in-call chat, and the E2EE pill that
only turns on when the media is really
sealed.
The safety number and the connection detail
(round trip, direct / relay) are on all
three.
The control bar itself matches: Speaker,
Mic, Camera, then group-only Participants /
Chat (one More button on the phones), then
End. Off is the loud state on all three.
The drift is inside the More menu. Android
still lists Raise hand and Share screen;
both write a flag only that device can see,
so the tile badge 'Sharing' is shown to
nobody. Web deleted them for exactly that
reason and the spec puts screen sharing out
of scope; iOS kept the fields and dropped
the controls.
'Low-data mode' on both phones promises
'Caps video at 360p'. Nothing reads the flag
- no media path on either platform mentions
it. Web removed the same toggle in the same
pass.
Same control, two names: 'Flip camera' on
the phones, 'Switch to the other camera' on
web.
14. Devices

g.text: See, add and remove the devices on this account.
The device you are using now.
The new device shows a code; scan it with this one.
Point the camera at the code your new
Point the camera at the code your new

svg.text: PARITY
Same list shape (this device marked, Remove
on the others) and the same pairing idea
(one device shows a code, the other scans
it).
Vocabulary split: web and iOS say 'Add a
device', Android says 'Link device' / 'Link
this device?'. The user reads one word on
the phone and another on the laptop for the
same act.
The recovery phrase, passkeys and the
authenticator sit behind Settings > Security
> Recovery on all three, not on this screen;
that page links back here through its 'Other
devices' row.
Only web offers both directions ('Scan a
code' and 'Show a code') in one place; the
phones scan only.
15. Settings

g.text: How you sign in, which devices can read your messages,
and how you get back in.
See, add and remove the devices on this account.
Your recovery phrase and the other ways back into your account.
(no Delete account here - it lives on Passkeys)

svg.text: PARITY
Same sections and same order on all three:
Profile, Security (Passkeys / Devices /
Recovery), Appearance, Media, About, then a
separated danger zone.
Web is master / detail with a section list;
the phones are one scrolling list with
section headers. Fine for the form factor,
but web nests Profile as a peer section
while the phones nest it under 'Account'.
Web has no Network section - anti-censorship
cannot work in a browser (ADR-0026). The gap
is real and correct; the UI never says so,
it just is not there.
Android's 'Delete account' is not in the
danger zone at all - it sits on the Passkeys
screen. Web and iOS put it in Settings >
Account. A destructive action in a place
nobody would look for it.

svg.text: PARITY
Same content and order on all three: the
phrase row (what it is for, 'Saved on this
device.', 'Show recovery phrase'), Passkeys
with the count and how many restore keys,
Other devices, an informational three-word
row with nothing to switch, then the
authenticator.
'Show recovery phrase' proves it is you in
three ways. Web asks for the account
password. iOS asks the device (Face ID,
Touch ID or the passcode) and refuses when
no passcode is set. Android asks the device
(fingerprint, face or screen lock) and falls
back to the account password when the device
has no screen lock.
Web puts 'Show recovery phrase' and 'Manage'
at the end of each row; the phones use a
button under the phrase row and whole-row
navigation for Passkeys and Other devices.
Android opens the page with a paragraph
explaining what the phrase and the other
ways do; web and iOS go straight to the
cards.
The authenticator is an open card with its
set-up button on web and iOS, and a
collapsed 'Authenticator app' row that
expands on Android.
